newsitem.title: USA: Clinton works hard to compile new cabinet.
newsitem.headline: Clinton works hard to compile new cabinet.

text.p: President Bill Clinton's re-election celebrations were short-lived as he faced the challenge of rearranging his cabinet and replacing a stream of high-level appointees who plan to leave his administration.
Clinton, who faces the possibility of having to fill at least four, and perhaps as many as six, cabinet vacancies, was expected to start naming the new officials on Friday.

White House adviser George Stephanopoulos said on Wednesday night the president would hold a news conference by the end of the week, probably on Friday, at which he was likely to name a replacement for White House Chief of Staff, Leon Panetta.
"I think you'll have that replacement named very soon," Stephanopoulos said on CNN's "Larry King Live."
"It is important to have the White House structure in place early on in the transition ... to make sure we have an orderly process of new cabinet announcements," he said.
Panetta has told Clinton he wants to return to California but has promised to stay on at the White House through the transition.

Stephanopoulos, one of the president's closest advisers, also has indicated he will leave. He said in the CNN interview he planned "to take a week to think about it on the beach" but added: "I've had a great run ... I'm probably going to move on to other things."

After a triumphant return to the White House on Wednesday and a dinner celebration with several hundred of the Democratic Party, Clinton on Thursday began to plan the makeup of his second administration.
Two top aides -- Secretary of State Warren Christopher and Defence Secretary William Perry -- have already told the president they will resign.

One official also said Commerce Secretary Mickey Kantor was making plans to return to private life, while Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary said she would leave. Others on the departure list could include Transportation Secretary Federico Pena, Housing Secretary Henry Cisneros and Education Secretary Richard Riley.
Christopher, 71, and Perry, 69, were pillars of Clinton's national security policy but their departures had long been expected.
Officials said Christopher was expected to keep his post until Clinton's inauguration on Jan. 20 while Perry may also return to private life within a few months once a successor is chosen.

U.N. Ambassador Madeleine Albright and former Sen. George Mitchell are considered leading candidates to succeed Christopher, while there has been much speculation that CIA Director John Deutch may take Perry's place.
Officials said Clinton planned to meet with his cabinet to discuss the changes on Friday.
The president basked in the glow of his commanding victory over Republican Bob Dole, but pleaded with the Republican-controlled Congress to work with him -- not against him.

"If we can recreate for the next four years the spirit that existed in Congress in the last six weeks (of the last term, when a number of compromise bills were approved) we can do great things," he told reporters.

Voters gave Clinton only a partial triumph. They re-elected him by a margin of 49 percent to 41 percent for Dole, but allowed the Republicans to call the shots in both houses of Congress -- a move that many predict will lead not to cooperation but to cut-throat political infighting and give-no-quarter investigations of White House scandals.

Republican Party Chairman Haley Barbour tried to play down differences with Clinton, but Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott of Mississippi said the newly elected Congress would hold hearings on the Democrats' campaign finances.
A multitude of congressional hearings already have been held and three investigations are underway by independent counsels probing Clinton, his wife, his aides and associates.

For Clinton, the list of still unresolved issues seems endless -- from the Whitewater land deal he and his wife Hillary invested in years ago to questions about possible obstruction of justice by people in his White House.
